rv.q: Alistair McDowell has undoubtedly come up with the goods again in this strange and beautiful play, a mix of sci-fi, folk myth and elegy for humanity.
Quite what is the question that drives this dazzling, audacious and elusive drama.
Vicky Featherstone’s production has great control in the way it slowly feeds us information, toying with the confusion it creates as myth and history collide.
McDowall’s control of form sharpens the theatrical friction of his intriguingly juxtaposed questions.
Yet there is too much windy writing for the play to sear. It is a series of fiery moments, sometimes glowing, but also guttering.
Unfortunately, so does the show and the two acts remain hard to reconcile.
For me, it fails to hit the spot the way X so ingeniously did.
Without a doubt, this is the best piece of new writing on the London stage today.
If you surrender to it, it's utterly exhilarating and absorbing.
But thanks to the stellar performances, the piece is likely to engage you throughout, even if it leaves you with more questions than answers.
Engagingly puzzling at first, this representation of myths that endure soon becomes tiring.
What’s the point of this artless waste of resources?
However, McDowall’s plot peters out in the second half, when the destinations become more important than the journey.

cn.t: McDowall's ambitious time-traveling epic divides critics with its genre-bending Victorian spiritualism-meets-sci-fi narrative. While some find it breathtaking and exhilarating, others deem it confusing hokum that tests patience.
